flashcards.q: Name the four mechanical reasons ClickHouse is fast.
flashcards.a: Columnar storage (scan only needed columns), sparse primary index (binary search over per-granule entries), compression on sorted columnar data (5-20x+), and vectorized execution (SIMD, block-at-a-time operators).

flashcards.q: What is the default index_granularity and what does it mean?
flashcards.a: 8192 rows per granule (adaptive since 19.x, targeting ~10MB uncompressed for wide rows). The sparse primary index stores one entry per granule, not per row.

flashcards.q: Is the MergeTree primary index unique or a B-tree?
flashcards.a: Neither. It's a sparse, sorted array of per-granule starting key values, binary-searched to find candidate granule ranges -- not a per-row structure and not a tree.

flashcards.q: What causes the 'Too many parts' error and what's the primary fix?
flashcards.a: Frequent small inserts create parts faster than background merges can absorb, hitting a protective ceiling (default ~3000 active parts/partition). Primary fix: batch inserts client-side (10K-500K rows per insert, every 1-2s) rather than raising the limit.

flashcards.q: Why does ClickHouse never merge parts across partitions, and what's the practical consequence?
flashcards.a: Partitions are physically separate directories of parts by design. Over-partitioning (e.g. per-minute or high-cardinality keys) multiplies independent small-part pools, each accumulating unmerged parts -- coarser partitioning (monthly vs daily) is a common fix for too-many-parts.

flashcards.q: Which three operations are memory-bound in ClickHouse (not streaming), and why?
flashcards.a: High-cardinality GROUP BY (hash table sized to distinct groups, not rows scanned), JOIN (right-hand table loaded fully into memory for the hash join), and unbounded ORDER BY (must hold or spill the whole result set).

flashcards.q: What's the difference in outcome between a query hitting max_memory_usage vs the server hitting the Linux OOM killer?
flashcards.a: max_memory_usage kills only the offending query with a clean exception. The Linux OOM killer (triggered if max_server_memory_usage_to_ram_ratio, default 0.9, is exceeded) can kill the whole clickhouse-server process, taking down every other running query too.

flashcards.q: How do you diagnose which query caused an OOM after the fact?
flashcards.a: Query system.query_log WHERE type = 'QueryFinish' ordered by memory_usage descending to find the actual offending query pattern rather than guessing from the OOM alert.

flashcards.q: How do you prevent a GROUP BY or ORDER BY from OOMing instead of failing outright?
flashcards.a: Enable max_bytes_before_external_group_by (or external_sort for ORDER BY) so the operation spills partial state to disk past a memory threshold, trading latency for not needing unbounded memory.

flashcards.q: Why are JOINs expensive in ClickHouse mechanically?
flashcards.a: The default hash join loads the entire right-hand table into an in-memory hash table before probing with the left side, so the right table's size (not overall query row count) drives memory pressure, and probing is row-level random access that breaks columnar-scan locality.

flashcards.q: What are the three recommended ways to avoid expensive live JOINs in ClickHouse?
flashcards.a: Put the smaller table on the right side of any join you must do, use a Dictionary engine (fully in-memory, O(1) lookup) for small frequently-joined dimension tables, and denormalize static large-dimension attributes onto the fact table at ingestion time.

flashcards.q: A ReplacingMergeTree table shows duplicate rows right after insert. Why, and how do you get a correct read immediately?
flashcards.a: Deduplication happens at merge time, not insert time, and merges haven't run yet. Query with FINAL to force on-the-fly deduplication (at real CPU/latency cost) rather than assuming upsert-on-write.

flashcards.q: Difference between a ClickHouse projection and a materialized view?
flashcards.a: A projection is an alternate physical layout of the SAME table that the optimizer transparently picks (no cross-table joins allowed). A materialized view is a trigger on insert that writes results into a SEPARATE target table, moving aggregation from query time to insert time.

flashcards.q: Name three shapes of workload where ClickHouse is the wrong choice.
flashcards.a: Point updates/deletes at OLTP frequency (mutations are heavyweight async part rewrites), high-concurrency transactional writes with many small inserts (triggers too-many-parts), and any need for multi-statement ACID transactions or strict single-row current-value consistency.

flashcards.q: Why does denormalizing make sense in ClickHouse when it's an anti-pattern in Postgres?
flashcards.a: Postgres has cheap, transactional row-level updates so keeping normalized data in sync is cheap; ClickHouse updates are expensive async mutations and joins are the expensive operation, so paying the ingestion-time cost of denormalized writes once beats paying a live-join cost on every query.
